resources.string: Right or wrong sentence?
The parser gets the tokens from the scanner. It must know which token sequences are valid sentences.
One of these sentences is badly written. Tap it.
After a plus, a number must come.
A number is missing after the plus.
Listing every correct sentence is impossible: there are infinitely many. And a regular expression is not enough, because it cannot match parentheses.
GRAMMAR
A context-free grammar is a short list of rewriting rules that generates every valid sentence.
The empty rule
A rule can have an empty right side. We write epsilon. Here, S goes to epsilon erases the S. I already replaced S with a S b.
Which of these is a sentence, only terminals, that comes from S? Tap it.
Replace the S in the middle with epsilon. What is left?
a b. a S b still has a nonterminal: it is a sentential form. And b a does not come from this grammar.
Rightmost
There is another order: the rightmost derivation always replaces the rightmost nonterminal. It is the one the bottom-up parser rebuilds, backwards.
In Tipo, Var and semicolon, which does the rightmost one replace first? Tap it.
Terminals are not replaced. Of the nonterminals, take the one on the right.
Var. The semicolon is a terminal, so Var is the rightmost nonterminal.
Which of these forms appears only in the rightmost derivation? Tap it.
In the rightmost one, the derivation replaces Tipo last.
Tipo, asterisk, id and semicolon. The leftmost one replaces Tipo first and goes through float Var.
Both reach the same sentence, with the same tree. Only the order of the replacements changes.
Deriving a sentence takes three steps. They stay here on screen.
1. Start from the start symbol.
2. Replace the leftmost nonterminal.
3. Repeat until only terminals are left.
In the form E plus E, which step picks the left E? Tap it.
One of the steps says which nonterminal to replace.
Correct. Step two: always the leftmost one.
Now you derive. The goal is the declaration up top.
Decl became Tipo, Var and a semicolon. Which one do you replace now?
Step two: the leftmost nonterminal.
Tipo comes first.
Which rule of Tipo leads to the goal? Tap it.
Look at the first word of the goal.
Tipo becomes float.
Var is left. In the goal, an asterisk comes before the id. Tap the rule.
Only one rule of Var starts with an asterisk.
Exactly. Only terminals are left, and they match the goal.
Three replacements, one at a time. This is the tree of the declaration.
What about int id id semicolon? Is it in the language?
Look for a rule that puts two ids in a row.
No rule puts two ids in a row.
With no derivation reaching it, the sentence is outside the language. That is how the parser reports a syntax error.
Which operation goes first?
Two plus three times four is fourteen, because the times goes first.
If someone adds first, the result changes. Tap the number they get.
Add two and three. Then multiply by four.
Twenty, not fourteen.
In the compiler, the shape of the tree the parser builds decides the order of the operations.
To show that a grammar is ambiguous, the recipe has three steps.
And the first example, n plus n times n? The fix uses two levels. E joins sums of T, and T joins products. Now the sentence has a single tree.
Why does times always end up deeper than plus? Tap the reason.
T only makes times, and plus stays in E
Times appears later in the sentence
The times rule comes last
Look at what each nonterminal can generate. Where can a plus appear?
Plus is only born in the rule of E, which sits above the T nodes. Inside a T only times fits. The deeper one runs first.
One level per precedence: the operator that binds tighter sits on the lower level. This is the grammar the Bridge will fix next.
1. Pick a sentence of the language.
2. Try to build two different trees for it.
3. Found two? The grammar is ambiguous.
One sentence gave a single tree. Does that prove the grammar is not ambiguous?
Another sentence may still have two trees.
Nice. One sentence is enough to prove ambiguity, but not the opposite.
Another grammar, now with minus only. The sentence is n minus n minus n.
In this tree, which minus happens first? Tap it.
The left minus first, as in school.
I found another tree for the same sentence. Here, which minus comes first?
Here the right minus comes first.
With nine, five and two, what does this tree give? Tap the number.
Do five minus two first. Then subtract the result from nine.
You got it. Six. The other tree gave two.
Two trees for the same sentence: by the recipe, the grammar is ambiguous. Here, on top of that, the results differ.
The fix: to the right of minus, the new rule accepts only an n. The recursion stays on the left only, and minus is left-associative.
With the new rule, how many trees does n minus n minus n have?
To the right of the minus, only an n fits.
Just one tree.
This is the only tree. Minus is left-associative, as in math.
In a top-down parser, each nonterminal becomes a function. The function follows the rule's right-hand side, from left to right.
Before reading any token, what does the function E do? Tap the line.
Look at the first line inside the function.
It calls itself without reading anything.
Two loops
On exams, the rule often has more than one alternative with a loop. Here E goes to E plus T, to E minus T, or to T.
Step one: which alternatives start with E itself? Tap all of them.
Look at the first symbol of each one. More than one can start with E.
The first two. So there are two alphas: plus T, and minus T. The T alone is the beta.
E goes to T E prime. And what does E prime look like? Tap the right rule.
Each alpha becomes an alternative of E prime. And epsilon closes the rule.
Plus T E prime, minus T E prime, or epsilon. Without the minus, the grammar loses subtraction. Without epsilon, it never ends.
Each alpha got its own alternative, and epsilon shows up only once. With three alphas, there would be three alternatives plus epsilon.
LEFT RECURSION
A rule whose right-hand side starts with its own left-hand side has left recursion. No top-down parser accepts that.
Now swap the plus for a minus. In the old grammar, the tree of nine minus five minus two leans left. Nine minus five sits at the bottom and goes first: the result is two.
In the new grammar, the same sentence gives a tree that leans right. Read literally, it would do five minus two first, and give six.
So does minus now group from the right? Tap the answer.
The new grammar generates the same sentences. The code that builds the result decides the arithmetic.
The language is the same, but the tree changed. The parser joins the pieces in a loop, from left to right. The result is two again. You will see that loop in the AST topic.
No
Yes
The fix has three steps. It works for any rule of this kind.
1. Split: A → A α loops, A → β does not.
2. Replace each A → β with A → β A'.
3. Create A' → α A' | ε.
Here, which alternative plays the beta, the one without the loop?
The beta does not start with E.
The n is the beta, and plus n is the alpha.
List of ids
A list of ids separated by commas. Now you do the fix.
Step one: which alternative starts with L itself? Tap it.
Look for the alternative whose first symbol is the L.
Correct. It has the loop. The comma and the id form the alpha.
Step two: what does the new rule for L look like? Tap it.
The part without the loop comes first. L prime goes at the end.
First the id, then the new rule.
Step three: what goes into L prime? Tap both alternatives.
The alpha followed by L prime, and epsilon to stop.
Comma and id repeat, and epsilon ends it.
Done. No rule starts with its own left side.
Does the new grammar still generate id comma id? Tap the answer.
First, L goes to id and L prime. Then comma, id and epsilon.
Exactly. The language stays the same.
Now the function for L reads an id before calling another function. With each call the input moves on, and the parser terminates.
A command can be an assignment or a call. Both start with id.
can't tell
Seeing only the id, which rule does the parser pick? Tap it.
Look at the first token of each rule.
A single token can't decide between the two.
Left factoring has four steps. They stay here on screen.
1. Find the longest common prefix α.
2. Replace the rules with A → α A'.
3. In A', put the rest of each rule.
4. Repeat while two rules start the same way.
Which step keeps what was left of each rule? Tap it.
The rest comes after the common prefix.
The rest becomes the alternatives of the new rule.
If and else
Now a case that shows up on exams: if with else and without else. One whole rule is the start of the other.
What is the longest common start of the two if rules? Tap it.
Compare symbol by symbol. Where does the first rule end?
The if S. The first rule ends there, and the second goes on with else.
After if S, what is left of each rule? Tap both leftovers.
The second rule leaves else S. The first leaves nothing. How do you write nothing?
The else S, and epsilon. When the rest is empty, it becomes epsilon in the new rule.
Done. Without epsilon in S prime, the if without else would vanish from the language.
Careful: it is still not LL(1). With else in the input, S prime has two rules. Factoring does not remove the dangling else ambiguity.
Commands
Three commands start with id: one assignment and two calls.
Step one: what is the longest common prefix of the three? Tap it.
Compare the second symbol of the three. It already differs.
Only the id is common to all three.
I factor out the id. The rest goes into the new rule.
In the new rule, two alternatives still start the same way. Tap both.
Look for two with the same first symbol.
You got it. Both start with an open parenthesis.
Step four: factor again. What does the new rule look like? Tap it.
The open parenthesis moves to the front. The rest goes down to another rule.
What comes after the parenthesis gets a rule of its own.
Done. No rule has two alternatives with the same start.
The parser is in the second rule and reads an open parenthesis. How many alternatives fit?
Count the alternatives that start with an open parenthesis.
Only one. The factored grammar is LL(1).
Factoring does not change the language. It only postpones the choice until the deciding token arrives.
